o: We remove the maximal suffix made entirely of vowels ('a','e','i','o','u') and return the remainder, which may be empty. Walk a pointer backward from the end while characters are vowels, then cut the string there. "idea" → strip 'e','a' → "id"; "day" ends in 'y', a consonant, so nothing changes; "aeiou" is all vowels, leaving "". With length ≤ 100, any linear method is instant; the only care points are the all-vowel case and correctly identifying the vowel set (note 'y' is not a vowel here).
k: Trimming trailing vowels is a backward scan until the first non-vowel.
The result can legitimately be the empty string.
'y' is a consonant for this problem despite its sound.

a.i: Move an index from the end toward the front while characters belong to the vowel set, then slice. One pass, constant extra space, and handles the all-vowel case naturally when the index reaches -1.
s: While i >= 0 and s[i] is a vowel, decrement i.
a.t: O(n) — the pointer moves at most n steps backward.
a.sp: O(n) for the returned slice (O(1) auxiliary).

a.i: A single anchored regular expression [aeiou]+$ matches exactly the trailing vowel run; substituting it with the empty string performs the trim declaratively. Equivalent semantics, minimal code.
s: Apply the pattern /[aeiou]+$/ anchored at the end.
Replace the match with "" and return the result.
a.t: O(n) — the regex engine scans the suffix region once.

w: The pointer scan is preferable in interviews: no regex-engine overhead and trivially adaptable (e.g., trim leading vowels too). Pitfalls: including 'y' in the vowel set, mishandling the fully-vowel input (must return ""), and in languages with immutable strings, remembering slicing allocates. Follow-ups: trim both ends, trim trailing vowels repeatedly until none remain (identical result), or operate on a character stream.
